c1.story:
Everything you own made a journey. The phone in your pocket arrived in a container at Nhava Sheva or Mundra, rode a train or truck to a warehouse near your city, sat on a shelf in a sorting hub and reached your door on a delivery rider's scooter. The coal that lit your bulb came through a bulk port and a rake of wagons. The cooking gas in your kitchen was unloaded at an LPG terminal on the west coast. Logistics is the plumbing of the economy, and like plumbing, nobody thinks about it until something breaks.

Here is what makes it tricky for investors: logistics is not one business but four, and they could hardly be more different. The first owns gateways, ports, airports and storage terminals, under concessions that run for decades. Adani Ports at Mundra, GMR at Delhi and Hyderabad, Aegis Vopak's tank farms. They charge a toll on everything that passes through. The second hauls containers on Indian Railways' tracks, like CONCOR, or builds railway lines for the state, like RVNL; the government is both landlord and customer. The third delivers parcels, millions of them a day, for e-commerce platforms and businesses: Delhivery, Shadowfax, Blue Dart. The fourth owns ships and rents them out at whatever the world market pays that week, like Great Eastern Shipping and the Shipping Corporation of India.

A port stock is a toll collector, a parcel stock is a price war, and a shipping stock is a commodity. The word logistics tells you none of this.

The same news hits them in opposite directions. A spike in global container rates delights a shipowner and annoys every importer using the ports. A surge in online shopping fills Delhivery's vans but barely moves Mundra. A bigger railway budget fills RVNL's order book and means nothing to a tanker owner. So before reading any number, decide which door the company walks through.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each top to bottom, then compare the bars, because this is one of the industries where the bars differ most.

  • The name and line under it tell you how the money is made: a fee per tonne, container, passenger or litre stored at a gateway; haulage and construction for a government customer; a few rupees per parcel; or a daily charter rate set by the world market.
  • The tickers are listed names mostly behind each door. Click one to open its stock page.
  • The bar shows how much profit the company keeps. Ports, airports and terminals sit at high: once the asset is built, extra volume costs almost nothing to handle. Rail freight and rail builders sit at medium. Shipping sits at medium on average, though in practice it swings from feast to famine. Express parcels sit at low: the platforms and the competition take most of the margin.
  • The last line is the bet: trade and travel volumes through a gate you own, the railway budget and the shift from road to rail, online shopping beating the price war, or world freight rates.

The analogy below makes it memorable: a toll bridge, carts on the government's road, a delivery boy paid per packet, and a cart owner renting at the market rate. The so-what line is the rule to carry everywhere: the word logistics on its own tells you nothing about what you are buying.

c2.story:
Follow a single container from a factory in Ludhiana to a buyer in Rotterdam, and you walk through the whole kitchen.

Station one is the origin: a factory, mine, farm or e-commerce seller with goods ready to move. Station two is the gateway. If the goods are leaving the country, they pass through a port like Mundra, Nhava Sheva or Pipavav; if they are fuel or chemicals, they may sit in a storage terminal run by Aegis. If they are travellers, the gateway is an airport like Delhi, run by GMR. Station three is the line haul, the long journey between hubs: by rail on Indian Railways' tracks, often in a CONCOR container train, by truck with one of millions of small owner-operators, or by sea, usually on a foreign shipping line. Station four is the hub and warehouse: inland container depots, sorting centres and warehouses where cargo is stored, sorted and dispatched. Station five is the last mile: the truckload reaching the factory or the parcel reaching your door.

Now look at who stands where. Indian listed companies hold the gateways, the hubs and the last mile, and that is where the profit pools are. The long-haul leg in the middle is dominated by the state railway on land and by foreign shipping lines at sea. India's containers mostly travel on ships owned by the likes of Maersk and MSC.

For years there was another leak: many of India's containers changed ships at Colombo, Singapore or Dubai, because Indian ports were not deep enough for the biggest vessels. That is why Vizhinjam, the deep-water transhipment port near Thiruvananthapuram, commissioned in 2025 and run by Adani, matters so much. It is India's first serious attempt to bring that business home.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row beneath them.

The boxes follow a shipment: origin, gateway, line haul, hub and warehouse, last mile. Each tells you what happens there and who stands there. Notice how the cast changes at the middle station: Indian listed names at the gateway, then Indian Railways, small truckers and foreign shipping lines for the long haul, then Indian listed names again at the hubs and the last mile.

The band row is unusual. Three of the five cells are coloured as Indian listed: the gateway, the hub and warehouse, and the last mile. The first cell belongs to shippers, the customers. The middle cell, line haul, is marked as a rival station, held by foreign shipping lines and the Railways.

So the picture is a listed industry with a hole in the middle. Indian investors can own the toll gates at either end and the delivery network, but mostly cannot own the long-haul leg.

  • A trade slowdown starts at station one and hits the gateways first.
  • A rail haulage hike or a freight-rate spike starts at station three and squeezes whoever is buying that leg.
  • An e-commerce slowdown hits stations four and five together.

The rival line names the transhipment hubs as competitors, and the note explains why Vizhinjam matters. The so-what line draws the investment conclusion: the gateways and the last mile are where listed names stand and where the profit pools are.

c3.story:
Logistics companies sell a service nobody wants for its own sake. Demand is derived from whatever the customer is moving, which means the customer list tells you almost everything about a logistics company's next quarter.

Exporters and importers buy port handling, container rail and shipping. Their volumes move with global trade, tariffs and the rupee, and since late 2023 with the Red Sea, where Houthi attacks forced many ships to sail around Africa, lengthening voyages and lifting freight rates. Coal, power and cement producers buy bulk port handling, rail wagons and coastal shipping; a hot summer that drives up power demand fills bulk berths and coal rakes. Oil, gas and chemical companies buy storage terminals and tankers: Aegis's LPG terminals on the west coast fill up as India imports more cooking gas.

E-commerce platforms are the parcel carriers' biggest customers, and also their most dangerous ones. Amazon, Flipkart and Meesho send huge volumes, but each has built its own logistics arm and can move volume in-house whenever it chooses. The rise of quick commerce, Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, has changed how goods move in cities, from big sorting hubs to small dark stores.

Manufacturers and FMCG companies buy truckload freight and warehousing; since GST in 2017 and the e-way bill in 2018, they have consolidated from a godown in every state to a few large regional warehouses. Air passengers are the airports' customers, moving with airline capacity and middle-class travel. Indian Railways itself is a customer, buying new lines, electrification and consulting from the rail builders, on the strength of its budget.

And finally automakers and agriculture: car carriers, cold chains, and bulk movement of grain and imported fertiliser around the harvest calendar.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines: who buys, what they buy, what moves them.

  • Trade and bulk tiles: exporters and importers, coal, power and cement, and oil, gas and chemicals. They move with global trade, power demand and fuel imports. These feed the gateway door.
  • Consumer tiles: e-commerce platforms and air passengers. They move with online shopping and travel.
  • Industrial tiles: manufacturers and FMCG, and automakers and agriculture. They move with industrial output, vehicle sales and harvests.
  • The government tile: Indian Railways, moving with its own budget.

The useful exercise is to map each tile to a door from card one. Ports and terminals read the trade and bulk tiles and the air passenger tile. Rail freight reads exporters and bulk; rail builders read only the Railways tile. Parcel carriers read the e-commerce and manufacturer tiles. Shipping reads trade and oil, but on a global rather than Indian scale.

Notice one tile that cuts both ways: e-commerce platforms are customers that can become competitors overnight by insourcing delivery. That is a risk no other tile carries.

The so-what line gives the habit: a port name reads the trade data and the coal numbers, a parcel name reads e-commerce order counts. Look at the customer before the quarter.

c4.story:
If you want to see how different logistics businesses really are, look at where each rupee goes. The contrast is the starkest on this whole page.

A port is a toll plaza. It costs a fortune to build: dredging, breakwaters, berths, cranes, rail links. Once built, it costs remarkably little to run. The variable costs, fuel for the equipment, handling labour and a share of revenue paid to the state under the concession, take only a small slice of each rupee. The big costs are depreciation on the asset and interest on the debt that paid for it. So every extra container is nearly pure profit, and the business has enormous operating leverage. That is why Adani Ports has historically reported operating margins that most industrial businesses can only dream of.

A parcel company is the opposite. It owns relatively little. It leases trucks, rents sorting hubs and pays delivery riders per shipment. Most of its revenue goes straight back out in line-haul costs, fuel, handling and rider payouts. What remains is thin, and every price cut by a competitor eats directly into it. Delhivery spent years after its 2022 listing getting to consistent profit, and its acquisition of Ecom Express in 2025 was partly a bet that consolidation would finally ease the price war.

A port earns little per rupee of asset, but for decades. A parcel network earns a lot per rupee of asset, but keeps almost none of it.

Shipping sits somewhere else entirely: a heavy asset, like a port, but with revenue that swings with world charter rates. A shipowner's fate turns on how much debt it carried into the downturn. Rail builders are different again: light assets but heavy working capital, because government clients pay slowly, and interest earned on client advances can be a surprisingly large share of profit.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a port or terminal and for an express parcel carrier. Put them side by side and they look like different universes.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is fuel, handling and concession fees. For the port it is small, about a seventh. For the parcel carrier it is enormous, roughly two thirds and more, because the carrier pays someone else for nearly every kilometre and every delivery.
  • The opex bar is people, power, maintenance and rent: about a fifth for the port and a quarter for the parcel carrier.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is where the port pays for its asset. It is the port's biggest cost, more than a quarter of sales. For the parcel carrier it is a thin sliver.
  • The last bar is what is left. The port keeps well over a third of each rupee. The parcel carrier keeps a few paise. It is the widest gap between two doors anywhere on this page.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover for amounts.

Below, the list marks which lines matter. Four get a clear yes: volume and realisation per unit, depreciation, interest and capex with asset turn. Four get a sometimes: working capital, fuel, rail haulage charges and other income. The so-what line tells you what to read per door: volume and margin for the toll collectors, shipments and cost per shipment for parcels, the day rate and debt for shipping.

c5.story:
Is logistics cyclical? The honest answer is: it depends which door. Shipping is violently cyclical, swinging with world freight rates. Ports and parcels are steady growers that wobble with trade and consumption. Rail builders follow the railway budget rather than any market cycle. But the last few years gave all four a shared ride.

It began with Covid. Lockdowns emptied ports for a quarter in 2020, then the world went on a shopping spree from home. Containers piled up in the wrong places, ships queued outside ports, and container freight rates multiplied several times. Indian shipping companies earned in a year what they used to earn in five. E-commerce volumes jumped. Delhivery listed in 2022 at a rich valuation, and the government launched the National Logistics Policy the same year, promising to cut India's logistics cost.

The peak came in 2022: rates topped out, everyone ordered ships and built warehouses. Then 2023 brought the bust. Freight rates fell back to pre-Covid levels, e-commerce growth slowed, parcel carriers undercut each other, and the listed start-ups lost more than half their value. Adani Ports had its own shock that January, when the Hindenburg report hit every Adani group stock, though its cargo kept growing.

The bottom was strange, because volumes never stopped growing. Port cargo kept hitting records. Then the Red Sea attacks from late 2023 forced ships around Africa and put a floor under freight rates. In 2024 railway PSU stocks went on a speculative run on budget hopes and then gave much of it back. In 2025 Vizhinjam opened, the western freight corridor neared completion, and quick commerce rewired urban delivery.

So the industry now sits in an early up-cycle, led by volume. The toll gates are compounding; the parcel price war has eased but not ended.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock shows boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The last cycle was short and sharp: boom from 2020 to 2022, peak in 2022, bust in 2023, bottom across 2023 and 2024. The arrow sits just past the bottom, heading into the boom arc, labelled early up-cycle, with volumes at records and parcel prices still weak. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019. Most entries are neutral, which is itself informative: this is a growth industry with one sharp boom and one sharp bust, in 2021 and 2022 and in 2023. The rest is steady building.

The four hands map onto the doors.

  • Port cargo growth: high single digits, arrow up. The gateways' engine, running well.
  • Container freight rates on India routes: off the highs, arrow down. Bad for shipping names, good for importers and the ports' customers.
  • Parcel yield per shipment: stabilising, flat. The price war has paused. Rising would mean it is over.
  • Railway capital budget and corridor progress: high but flat. A flat budget caps the rail builders' order inflow.

One up, one down, two flat. Each door is at a different point, and only the ports' hand is clearly pointing up. That is exactly what the so-what line says: the toll collectors benefit first, parcels only when pricing recovers, shipping only if world rates hold.

c6.story:
Logistics is the economy's circulation, so its dials are mostly measures of how much stuff is moving. Two dials carry maximum weight, and they are both about volume.

The first is India's trade: exports and imports passing through the ports. Every container that leaves Mundra or arrives at Nhava Sheva is a fee for the port, a load for a container train and often a parcel or truckload downstream. The second is core-sector output: coal, cement and steel. These are the bulk cargoes, tonnes rather than boxes, that fill bulk berths and freight trains. A hot summer that drives up power demand, and with it coal movement, shows up quickly at bulk ports and on the railways.

Then come the medium dials. Industrial output drives truckload and warehouse demand. Online shopping growth drives parcel volumes. Government capex on rail and ports fills the rail builders' order books and adds new terminals. Interest rates matter for the heavy-asset owners: ports, airports, ships and wagons are funded with long-term debt.

For a toll collector, the only thing better than more trucks is more trucks on a road someone else has already paid for.

And the two-faced dials. Crude oil raises diesel, bunker and aviation fuel costs, hurting truckers and parcel carriers, but it also lifts tanker demand and rates, helping owners like Great Eastern Shipping. Global freight rates and the Red Sea route boost shipowners and hurt every shipper paying them. The rupee helps shipping companies, which earn in dollars, and raises costs for anyone importing.

Notice what is missing from the heavy row: prices. For most of this industry, volume is the story and price is a secondary concern. The exception is shipping, where price, the day rate, is almost everything.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel, what a rise does, and its weight in dots.

  • Green upward arrows mean a rise helps. They dominate this table: trade volumes, core-sector output, online shopping, industrial output, government capex and imports.
  • Red downward arrows mean a rise hurts. Only one: interest rates, which squeeze leveraged asset owners.
  • Diamonds mean mixed: crude oil, global freight rates and the rupee. Each helps one door and hurts another.

So many green arrows tell you something: this is a volume industry that mostly benefits when the economy grows. That is rare on this page.

Count the three-dot rows: trade volumes and core-sector output. Both are volume dials, both feed the gateway door most directly.

The last column shows today's reading where a series is tracked: India's exports and imports, the core-sector index, Brent crude, the money market rate, the rupee, industrial output and the infrastructure index for government capex. Online shopping growth and global freight rates show a dash; for those, read platform festive-sale commentary and the container rate indices published weekly by shipping analysts.

The so-what line simplifies it to two dials: port cargo growth for volume and crude for cost. For a shipping name specifically, add a third, the freight rate row, because it decides almost everything for that door.

c7.story:
India's logistics costs have long been higher than they should be for an economy its size. The bottlenecks explain why, and they also explain which listed companies benefit as each one slowly gets fixed.

Start with the structural ones. Indian Railways owns the track, sets the haulage charge and runs its own freight trains. Private container train operators, CONCOR included, are tenants on the landlord's track, and a haulage hike can wipe out a year's margin overnight. The government has talked for years about selling its stake in CONCOR, but the landlord relationship stays whatever happens to the ownership. Fragmented trucking is the other structural one: millions of owner-drivers with one or two trucks set a brutal price floor, and no organised player can hold a premium for long.

Then the slow-moving ones, which are the real long-term story. Most cargo still goes by road, which is slower and costlier than rail; the dedicated freight corridors, the eastern one complete and the western one nearly so, are meant to shift it. Transhipment has leaked abroad to Colombo and Singapore for decades; Vizhinjam is the first real answer. Both are fixing themselves, but over a decade, not a quarter.

Logistics bottlenecks are the investment case for ports and corridors, and the investment risk for everyone else.

The recurring bites are the quarter-level surprises. Concession disputes can reset a port or airport's economics: a tariff ruling, a revenue-share fight, a land battle. Seasonality bunches cargo and parcels into the second half of the year, around the harvest and festivals. And government bills paid late bloat rail builders' receivables, making profit a function of cash collection rather than work done.

The cyclical one is the parcel price war. Every time a new network gets funded, or a platform expands its own fleet, yields fall.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you how to treat each risk.

  • Structural: rail haulage and track access, and fragmented trucking. Permanent. The first caps container rail returns; the second caps any organised road player's pricing.
  • Slow: road share too high, and transhipment leaking abroad. Both are slowly improving, and that improvement is the long-term tailwind for rail corridors and Indian ports. Notice that these slow rows are opportunities as much as constraints.
  • Recurring: concession and regulatory risk, seasonality, and late government payments. These are the headlines that move single stocks for a quarter.
  • Cyclical: parcel price wars, which return whenever fresh funding enters the market.

Read the table with the doors in mind. Ports and terminals mostly face the recurring concession risk and benefit from the slow transhipment fix. Rail freight faces the structural haulage risk and benefits from the slow road-to-rail shift. Parcel carriers face the cyclical price war and fragmented trucking. Rail builders face late government payments.

The so-what line puts it plainly: the first two rows are why ports and corridors are the long-term story, and the sixth is why parcel names keep disappointing. For a parcel stock, the single most useful news alert is any fresh funding round for a rival network or any platform announcing it will deliver more in-house.

c8.story:
Much of Indian logistics runs on government land, government track and government licences, so the rulebook is not background noise. It is the business model.

The most important document for any private port is its concession agreement with a state maritime board. It grants the right to build and run a port for decades, sets the revenue share paid to the state, and spells out what the operator may charge. The moat and the risk of every private port name live in that one document. Adani Ports' strength at Mundra rests on Gujarat's maritime board concession; its newer ports rest on agreements with other states. The ministry of ports, shipping and waterways runs the big state-owned major ports, sets their tariffs and drives the Sagarmala programme. Major ports are the private ports' direct competitors, so their pricing sets the benchmark.

The ministry of railways is the landlord and the customer at once. It owns the track, sets haulage charges, runs the freight corridors through a dedicated company, and buys new lines and electrification from the rail builders. The Airport Economic Regulatory Authority fixes aeronautical charges at the big airports in five-year blocks, so a single tariff order can swing GMR's earnings for years.

Some rules reshaped the industry quietly. GST in 2017 and the e-way bill in 2018 killed the state-border checkposts where trucks once queued for hours and let companies consolidate warehouses. The National Logistics Policy and PM GatiShakti coordinate where corridors, multimodal parks and warehouses get built.

And the newest push is maritime. The 2025 budget set up a maritime development fund, shipbuilding gets subsidies and finance, and a coastal shipping law aims to grow Indian-flag shipping. Cabotage rules and a right of first refusal for Indian ships protect shipowners' home market from foreign lines.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and status.

  • Always: six rows, the ports ministry and major port authorities, port concession agreements, the railways ministry and the freight-corridor company, the airport tariff regulator, GST with the e-way bill, and cabotage rules. Six permanent fixtures is a lot; it reflects how much of this industry runs on government assets and licences.
  • Live: the National Logistics Policy with PM GatiShakti, and the Competition Commission, which watches the largest port operator's acquisitions and the platforms' logistics arms.
  • New: shipbuilding assistance and the maritime development fund. A slow tailwind for Indian-flag shipping and domestic yards.

There is no coming row on this card, which is worth noticing. The big rules are in place; what matters now is how they are applied.

Read the rows against the doors. Ports care most about concession agreements and the ports ministry. Airports care about the tariff regulator. Rail freight and rail builders care about the railways ministry. Parcel carriers care about GST and the Competition Commission's view of platforms. Shipping cares about cabotage and the new maritime push.

The why column flags the single most important document for each door. For a port name, that is the concession; for a container rail name, the haulage charge schedule.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Porter's five forces asks who keeps the money. In logistics, the answer depends entirely on whether you own something that cannot be replicated.

Consider a port. To compete with Mundra, a rival needs a deep coastline, a concession from a state government, environmental clearances, rail and road links, and a decade of construction. Nobody can build a second coastline. Rivalry exists, but it is with the next port a few hundred kilometres away, and the gateway that has the best hinterland links and the deepest berths wins. Shipping lines negotiate hard, but they need somewhere to dock. Suppliers barely matter: a port buys little except power, equipment and dredging. Substitutes are slow: cargo can shift ports or modes, but only over years.

Now consider a parcel carrier. It competes with every other carrier and with its own customers' in-house fleets. Amazon, Flipkart and Meesho can insource delivery whenever they like, and they dictate rates to the carriers they do use. Suppliers, gig workers, fuel sellers and leased-truck owners, have prices the carrier does not set. And a new network needs only funding and a year. Shadowfax built a gig-delivery network precisely by being lighter than the incumbents.

The gateway owner keeps the profit because nobody can build a second coastline. The parcel carrier hands its profit to the platforms.

That is why ports are valued as long-duration compounders and parcel carriers as perpetual turnaround stories. Delhivery's purchase of Ecom Express in 2025 was an attempt to shrink the rivalry spoke by removing a competitor. Whether consolidation can hold pricing when platforms keep building their own networks is the open question for the parcel door.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches, the more pressure. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes: ports, airports and terminals, and express parcels. Look at size first. This is the most lopsided radar on the page. The ports shape is tiny, hugging the centre. The parcels shape sprawls outward on every spoke.

Now read spoke by spoke.

  • Entrants: the port score is the lowest mark on the chart, half a point. Nobody can build a second coastline. Parcels score high, because a new network needs only funding.
  • Rivalry: ports low, parcels at the maximum of three.
  • Buyers: ports low to moderate, parcels at the maximum. The platforms dictate rates.
  • Suppliers: ports low, parcels moderate.
  • Substitutes: both relatively low, the one spoke where the shapes come close. Cargo shifts slowly; but a platform can insource delivery overnight.

Two maximum scores for parcels, rivalry and buyers, is the business in one picture: competitors on one side, powerful customers on the other.

The table beside the chart gives each score with a reason. If you own a rail freight or shipping name, neither shape applies directly. Try redrawing: container rail would show a high supplier spoke, because the Railways is the landlord, while shipping would show high rivalry, because the world market sets the rate.

c10.story:
Logistics results calls are full of operational detail: berths commissioned, rakes added, hubs opened, pin codes covered. Eight numbers tell you whether the network is earning.

Volume growth comes first, in tonnes, containers or parcels. For ports, high single digits to low double digits is healthy; for parcels, faster growth is expected because the market itself is younger. Then realisation per unit, pricing power per tonne, container or parcel. For ports, realisation should rise roughly with inflation under the tariff structure. For parcels, the vital question is whether yield per shipment is flat or rising, or falling again, which means the price war has restarted.

Then the margin. EBITDA margin shows the asset's operating leverage, and the benchmarks differ wildly by door: very high for ports, solid for container rail, single digits and rising for express.

Next, the debt numbers, because this is an asset-heavy industry. Debt to EBITDA shows whether the asset's debt is comfortable; interest to EBITDA shows how much of operating profit the lenders take. For shipping, debt at the top of the cycle is the number that decides survival at the bottom.

Then capex against depreciation. Building new capacity makes sense when utilisation is high; building into empty berths or half-full hubs is how returns get diluted. Receivable days tell you whether customers are paying: short for ports, where customers often pay upfront, and longer for rail builders waiting on government bills.

And finally return on capital, the summary. Ports should earn comfortably above their cost of capital once mature; parcel carriers should at least be positive and improving; rail builders should earn well, given how light their assets are.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask each company.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures, and almost every row gives separate marks per door: ports, container rail, express, shipping, rail builders. Always read the mark for the right door. A parcel carrier's margin judged against a port's benchmark will always look terrible, and that comparison tells you nothing.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It is shown for EBITDA margin, debt to EBITDA, interest to EBITDA, capex to depreciation, receivable days and return on capital.

Two rows show a dash: volume growth and realisation per unit. They are not in annual filings. For ports, read the monthly cargo data the companies and the ports ministry publish. For parcels, read shipment counts and yield in investor presentations.

One caution on medians in this industry: the listed universe mixes toll collectors, rail builders, parcel carriers and shipowners, so an industry median blends very different economics. It is most useful for the balance-sheet rows, debt and interest cover, where the question is the same for every door. For the margin and return rows, compare each company to its door's good mark and its own history.

c11.story:
Logistics has one big advantage for investors: much of its data is published before the results. Ports report monthly cargo. The commerce ministry publishes trade figures. Coal stocks at power plants are tracked closely. E-commerce platforms talk about festive sales. Shipping analysts publish container and tanker rate indices weekly. The railway budget comes once a year. Property consultants track warehouse leasing.

Each speaks with a different lead time. Port cargo and trade data are the same quarter: tonnage is revenue, and containers move with trade the same month. Coal and power demand, e-commerce order commentary, global freight rate indices and crude speak one quarter ahead. The railway budget and freight-corridor commissioning, and warehouse leasing data, speak two quarters ahead, because budget lines take time to become orders and new warehouse space takes time to fill.

Combine them and you get a three-part test. The industry is in an up-cycle when port cargo is growing, parcel yields are stable or rising, and freight rates are holding. Three of three is a boom. Two is a volume-led recovery. One is a false dawn.

Right now two are true. Port cargo is at records, growing in the high single digits. Parcel yields are stabilising as the price war eases. The missing sign is freight rates, which have come off the Red Sea highs.

That shapes the call: a volume-led early up-cycle, favouring the toll collectors, ports and terminals, over parcel carriers and shipping until parcel pricing and freight rates both turn. For rail builders, the call's advice is to watch order inflow rather than the PSU label. And what could change it: a global trade or tariff shock cutting container volumes, a fresh funded entrant reopening the parcel price war, or a rail haulage hike or concession dispute hitting a listed operator.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for its channel.

  • Same quarter: monthly port cargo data and export and import data. They are published before results, so the ports' quarter is largely known in advance.
  • One quarter ahead: coal and power demand, e-commerce order value and festive-sale commentary, global container and tanker rate indices, and crude oil.
  • Two quarters ahead: the railway budget and freight-corridor commissioning, and warehouse leasing data. The earliest warnings, and they mostly matter for rail builders and contract logistics.

Use it door by door. A port investor lives on the left-hand dots, which are almost a live feed of revenue. A parcel investor watches the e-commerce dot in the middle. A shipping investor watches the rate indices. A rail builder investor watches the rightmost dot, the budget.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. Two ticks: port cargo growing at records, and parcel yields stabilising as the price war eases. One cross: freight rates are off the Red Sea highs. Two of three is what the rule calls a volume-led recovery.

The call box gives the view and what would change it: a trade or tariff shock, a funded parcel entrant, or a haulage hike or concession dispute. Treat them as alerts. Each maps to one door, so if one fires, you know which holding to revisit.
